chunks: What EMI shields connect to, and why. The question: What are EMI shields typically connected to? Why?
A shield only works if it is connected to the right place in the right way. A shield can on a board connects to the circuit's ground plane, all the way around its edge.
A cable shield or metal enclosure connects to the chassis, the product's metal frame, through the connector shell. A floating shield passes noise on.
Think of a bathtub. Noise current is water pouring in, and the shield's voltage is the water level. A wide, short drain keeps the level low.
A narrow, long drain, like a thin wire pigtail, lets the level rise until it overflows into the room, which is the sensitive circuit.
A tub with no drain, a floating shield, fills right up.
The noise source drives a displacement current through C s into the shield node.
A low-impedance Z g (short, wide ground connection) drains it to ground, so the shield node barely moves and the victim sees almost nothing through C v .
If Z g is large (a long pigtail) or absent (floating), the shield node swings and drives the victim.
Ground plane: a solid copper layer at 0 volts inside the board. Chassis: the metal frame or enclosure of the product.
Floating: connected to nothing, so its voltage drifts with whatever couples to it. Pigtail: a single thin wire used to connect a shield, which has a lot of inductance.
Inductance: how strongly a wire resists fast current changes. At 100 megahertz, a 10 nanohenries wire acts like about 6 ohms.
Say a noisy node swings 12 volts at 2. 4 volts per nanosecond, and a stray 1 picofarads capacitance (nearby metal passing fast voltage changes) links it to the shield.
That pushes a current of 1 picofarads times 2. 4 volts/ns = 2. 4 milliamps into the shield. At 100 megahertz, a 10 nanohenries pigtail is about 6.
3 ohms, so the shield swings about 15 millivolts. A connection through many short plated holes (vias), about 0. 5 nanohenries, is about 0. 3 ohms, which gives only about 0.
75 millivolts. A floating shield, with 5 picofarads to ground, would swing about 2 volts. That is the whole idea: give the noise current a short, wide way home.

"Board-level cans are connected to the PCB ground plane at many points around the perimeter; cable shields and enclosures are bonded to chassis with a 360 degree low-inductance connection at the connector.

Shielding an electric field means giving the displacement current a path to return, so the shield has to be grounded, and at RF the connection impedance matters: 10 nanohenries is 6 ohms at 100 megahertz.
A floating shield just floats to some potential and re-couples noise. For cables, RF wants both ends bonded; low-frequency audio may need one end to avoid ground loops."
Quick check. Why must an electric-field shield be connected to ground?
